chapter.title: Running it every day without you

cards.body: Your clipping person is good, but so far you have had to walk into the office each morning and say "go". Today you hand over a key and an alarm clock. **At 7am they let themselves in, read the 5 papers, and leave the note on your desk whether or not you are there.** You find it next to your coffee.
cards.simpler: Picture a helper who reads the newspapers for you. Until now, you had to walk in each morning and tell them to start. Today you give them a key and an alarm clock. **At 7am they let themselves in, read the 5 papers, and leave a note on your desk, whether you are there or not.** When you arrive, the note is waiting next to your coffee.

cards.prompt: Your clipper's note is excellent. But they leave it in a locked filing cabinet in the basement. You never read it. What is the problem?

options.text: The note lands somewhere you never look

whyNot.a: That's the summary's length, which chapter 5 handled: a 2-sentence note is short enough. The trouble here is where it ends up.
whyNot.c: That's a speed problem, and the agent takes seconds either way: the note is written fine, it is just put where you won't see it.

cards.reteach: An agent that runs on time but writes to a place you never open is the same as an agent that never ran. Half of "running without you" is the alarm clock. The other half is the note landing where your eyes already go each morning.

cards.title: The alarm clock
cards.body:
So far you have typed a command to run each step. A *scheduler* is a small program on your computer or a server that runs a command for you at a set time, every day, with nobody typing anything.

On a Mac or Linux machine the built-in scheduler is called *cron*. You give it 2 things: a time, like 7:00 each morning, and the command to run. It keeps doing that until you tell it to stop.

**One schedule, one command.** That command should run all 3 steps in order: fetch, compare, summarise. If they are 3 separate scripts today, wrap them in 1 script first, so the clock only has to ring once.
cards.simpler: So far you have typed each command yourself. A scheduler is a small program that runs commands at set times, like an alarm clock. On a Mac or Linux computer the built-in one is called cron. You give it a time and a command, and it repeats that daily until you stop it. **One schedule, one command.** That command should run all 3 steps in order: fetch, compare, summarise. If they are 3 separate scripts, join them into 1 first.

cards.title: The note before standup
cards.body:
Say you track 4 rivals and want the note before a 9am standup. You put 1 line in cron: run track.sh at 7:00. That script fetches the 4 pricing pages, compares them with yesterday's saved copies, and sends only the changed lines to the model.

The model's 2 sentences go into an email to yourself with the subject "Rival clippings, 4 Oct". Monday's email says: "No changes on 4 pages." Tuesday's says one rival cut its Starter plan from $29 to $19, and quotes the line. You read it on your phone in the coffee queue. **You did not open a terminal.**
cards.simpler: Say you watch 4 rivals and want the note by 9am. You add 1 line to cron: run track.sh at 7:00. It fetches the pricing pages, compares them with yesterday's copies, and sends the changed lines to the model. Its 2 sentences land in your inbox. Monday's says: "No changes on 4 pages." Tuesday's says one rival cut its Starter plan from $29 to $19. You read it on your phone in the coffee queue. **You never opened a terminal.**

cards.prompt: You set cron to run the fetch script at 7:00 and the compare script at 7:01. Some mornings the summary says "no changes" even though a page did change. What most likely happened?

options.text: The fetch sometimes takes over 1 minute, so compare ran before the new copy existed

whyNot.b: That's a model failure, chapter 7 territory: here nothing new ever reached the model, because compare looked at an old copy.
whyNot.c: That's a schedule setting, not a timing clash: cron runs at the time you give it every day, weekends included, unless you say otherwise.

cards.reteach: The clock should ring once and start one script that does the 3 steps in order. Two alarms 1 minute apart are a race: if step 1 is slow, step 2 starts with yesterday's copy and finds nothing new.

cards.title: Where the note lands
cards.body:
The second half is delivery. The scheduler can run your agent at 7:00 forever, but if the result sits in a file on a server, you will check it for 3 days and then forget. **Deliver to a place you already open every morning.**

The simplest 3 are: an email to yourself, a message in the chat app your team already uses, or a file in a folder that syncs to your phone. Email is the easiest start, because many small free tools can send one from a script.

Keep the subject line boring and the same every day, with the date on the end. Then, the one morning it says something new, you will notice.
cards.simpler: Delivery is the second half. A note left in a file on a server gets forgotten within days. **Send the note somewhere you already look every morning.** Try an email to yourself, your team's chat app, or a folder that syncs to your phone. Email is the simplest start, because small free tools can send one from a script. Keep the subject line the same every day, with the date on the end, so the one new morning stands out.

cards.body: A founder set the agent to run at midnight on their laptop, writing to a file called today.txt. Then they closed the lid, and a sleeping laptop does not run cron: for 9 days the file never changed, and they read the same "no changes" line 9 times. **Spot it by putting the date inside the message** and checking it matches today. Run the clock on a machine that stays awake, or on a small always-on server.
cards.simpler: A founder set the agent to run at midnight on their laptop, writing to a file called today.txt. Then they closed the lid. A sleeping laptop does not run cron, so for 9 days the file never changed, and they read the same "no changes" line 9 times without noticing. **Put the date inside the message** and check it matches today. Run the clock on a machine that stays awake, or on a small server that is always on.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a complete "running without you" setup, in the newspaper-clipping picture?

options.text: The clipper has a key and an alarm, and leaves the note on your desk
The clipper has an alarm but waits for you to unlock the door
The clipper has a key and leaves the note in the basement

whyNot.b: That's the schedule without the self-running part: an alarm that needs you at the door is still you typing the command each morning.
whyNot.c: That's the schedule without delivery: the agent ran, but the note is in a place you never look, so it may as well not have.

cards.reteach: Two halves, both needed. The alarm clock plus the key means the agent starts and finishes on its own. The note on the desk means the result is pushed to a place you already check, not a place you must remember to visit.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **A scheduler like cron runs your one script at the same time each day, with no one at the keyboard.** The script ends by sending its 2-sentence note, with the date in it, to a place you already open each morning, so you can tell at a glance that the clock really rang.
cards.simpler: **A scheduler like cron runs your one script at the same time each day, with nobody at the keyboard.** The script finishes by sending its 2-sentence note, with the date inside, to a place you already open each morning. That way you can see at a glance that the alarm really went off. If the date is old, you know something stopped.

cards.body: Tonight, pick the time. Open your calendar and find the 15 minutes you most reliably check email each morning. Write that down. Your cron time is 30 minutes before it.
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick the time. Open your calendar and find the 15 minutes each morning when you most reliably check email. Write that time down. **Your cron time is 30 minutes before it**, so the note is waiting when you look.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now set the agent to run once a day on its own and receive the summary without opening a terminal.
